newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Southern Africa sees bumper maize crop after rain.
newsitem.headline: Southern Africa sees bumper maize crop after rain.

text.p: Good rains should see southern Africa producing another bumper maize crop in the coming season, with the exception of Zambia where fertiliser shortages will hit hard, industry officials said on Wednesday.

Giel van Zyl, general manager of the National Maize Producers Organisation (NAMPO) in South Africa -- the biggest maize producer in the region -- said growers were banking on a second successive big crop following soaking rains.
"The crop is looking good at the moment," Van Zyl told Reuters, noting South African producers had reported good conditions for planting and for growing.
South Africa's National Crop Estimates Committee has put the 1996 maize crop at 9.48 million tonnes, more than double 1995's drought-reduced 4.41 million tonnes.
Van Zyl said it was too early to make predictions on the final size of the 1997 harvest.
However, Zambia expects a substantial drop in maize production due to a fertiliser shortage caused by a government liquidity crisis in 1996.
The country's National Union of Farmers said earlier this week it expected the maize crop to drop by 40 percent.

"Due to the late delivery of fertiliser and the inability of farmers to use expensive credit fertiliser, the maize yield is expected to drop by 40 percent to around nine and 10 million 90-kg bags," farmers union chief Ajay Vashee told Reuters.

About 49,000 tonnes of fertiliser worth $26 million had been ordered from South Africa but agriculture permanent secretary Austin Sichinga said the late arrival of the fertiliser was likely to have an adverse impact on the yield.
Zambia produced 15 million 90-kg bags of the staple maize last year, against a national requirement of 12 million.
Both Zimbabwe and Mozambique expect bumper harvests for the second year running.
Zimbabwe industry officials said maize output could rise by up to 13 percent.
The country's Commercial Grains Producers chairman Ian Gibson said he expected Zimbabwe's production to increase 13 percent to about three million tonnes from 2.6 million tonnes produced last year.
"Things are looking good. (Maize) seed sales are up 10 to 13 percent so we could have a similar increase in crop yields," Gibson said.
Zimbabwe -- which was hit by drought in 1995 -- has had good rains so far with most of its major reservoirs now 70 percent full.

In Mozambique, where the agriculture sector had been hard hit by 16 years of civil war, U.N. experts said they were upbeat on crop prospects and expected a record cereal harvest for the second year running.

"Last year we had 1.37 million tonnes and in 1997 we will have not less than 1.50 million tonnes of maize, millet, sorghum and rice," said Antonio Olivares, chief technical adviser to the Ministry of Agriculture's early warning system in Maputo.
"It's going to be better. The weather conditions in the whole country are good," said Olivares, who works for the U.N. Food and Agricultural Organisation.
Last year the harvest was limited by serious flooding.
"If we don't have floods this year you can add another 100,000 tonnes to the figure," Olivares said.
